#171349. Tech Report: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1039 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
  • No company has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
  • Industry observers note that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the firm selling the media sitting in the room.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

No company has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

Industry observers note that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the firm selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

So what changed? TTD latched onto a new principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the firm built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

Sources indicate that as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

If The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a newly introduced era for the firm:.

1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The organization should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

Sources indicate that 2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

From the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data remarked it would work for the buyer.

TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the company’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

According to recent reports, the business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

In 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

Industry observers note that redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

Advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

Industry observers note that the concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

Television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

Industry observers note that advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

None of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only organization in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

In a recent development, most turnarounds require a manufacturer to find a latest reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
  • In a recent development, now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
  • At the crux of the organization is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

In a recent development, now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

At the crux of the organization is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

Indeed, it’s the crux of the company name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

In September, it launched its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

Industry observers note that stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” said Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

Coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

It has been revealed that for this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” stated Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

In a recent development, based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène stated. It then validated the decision by testing the latest designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

Industry observers note that but rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, remarked Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

Industry observers note that when your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

Recent findings suggest that but no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, said Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

In a recent development, an AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” remarked Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

Industry observers note that stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell people what they want to hear, said Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

According to recent reports, having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène mentioned. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

Tech Report: OpenAI’s New Shopping Strategy; What Advertisers Are Thankful For

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.
  • So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.
  • The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

In a recent development, other changes to the documentation are less important, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

Marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search consumers. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

Sources indicate that plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently released “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

But AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

In a recent development, on Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

All that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

In a recent development, it’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for consumers.

Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research says that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

Ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

While the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

Would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

Sources indicate that microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

After Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the organization has appointed its new CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

Agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

According to recent reports, CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].

Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.
  • It’s a head-scratcher, says Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.
  • “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.

It’s a head-scratcher, says Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.

“Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he notes.

Industry observers note that in a principal media deal, an agency isn’t just advising a client; it’s selling to them. The agency buys media in bulk with its own money, then resells it to the client – usually without saying what’s in the package or what it paid – and then keeps the difference.

Which raises an obvious question: Is the agency recommending what’s best for its client or what’s best for the agency?

It has been revealed that to understand how the industry got here, Asghar states, you have to go back around 25 years to when media buying was unbundled at the behest of procurement and agencies started pooling client dollars to gain leverage. The original idea was to pass along the savings.

But after the ANA’s K2 report came out in 2016, it became clear that agencies were holding onto big volume rebates for themselves.

“They’re not actually savings; they’re profit,” Asghar says. “And they’re about the purest form of profit a company could attribute to their bottom line.”.

Sources indicate that today, holding companies have repackaged those rebates as principal deals, which is really just arbitrage. Asghar argues that this money should go back to the client.

In a recent development, not that any of this is happening secretly, though. Defenders of principal media like to say it’s fine as long as clients opt in. But Asghar isn’t buying it.

It has been revealed that “It’s one thing to know it’s happening,” he indicates. “It’s another thing to know what’s happening inside of what’s happening.”.

In other words, marketers can sign off on a principal deal and still have no idea what ended up on the plan. They often can’t get log-level data showing where their ads ran or what they originally cost. And because agencies buy the inventory at undisclosed discounts or through volume rebates before reselling it at a markup, the true price is hidden.

Marketers should go back to buying media separately from planning and strategy services, Asghar says, so the agencies giving advice aren’t also the ones with inventory to move.

Otherwise, Asghar says, an agency isn’t really acting as an agent.

Being a fiduciary, he says, “means you have a responsibility to do what’s in the best interest of [clients], not just what’s in the best interest of you or your shareholders.”.

Sources indicate that also in this episode: Why AI is going to “make dumb companies dumber and smart companies exceptional,” why young planners still need to learn the old-fashioned way even if agents can do some of their work for them and why attribution and measurement are the “dry turkey” of ad tech. (It “looks great on the outside,” Asghar quips, “but it’s terrible on the inside.”).

Healthcare Ads Are Coming To ChatGPT

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When OpenAI announced in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.
  • But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.
  • On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, unveiled its ChatGPT ads offering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When OpenAI announced in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.

But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.

On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, unveiled its ChatGPT ads offering.

WebMD Ignite serves hospitals and healthcare providers with agency solutions as well as content and data solutions, including its own DSP. Now, its agency offerings will include the opportunity to launch ads in ChatGPT.

Sources indicate that chatGPT Ads’ most recent ad policies provide more explicit detail on what is and isn’t permitted within healthcare advertising and offer more leeway than before. At least, there’s more leeway in the US – heath-related ads are still “generally prohibited” in other countries, according to the policy.

The ad policy also states that regulated products and services are still prohibited writ large, as are “claims related to the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of physical or mental health conditions.”.

However, OpenAI may accept ads on a case-by-case basis for less regulated offerings, including hospital and urgent care, health insurance, dietary supplements and consumer medical devices, wearables and apps.

Of WebMD Ignite’s clients, OpenAI has thus far only permitted ads from health systems and providers (like hospitals and academic medical centers), but not insurance companies.

Over 30% of Americans have used AI chatbots for health advice or information, so medical providers want to ensure that they’re “present and discoverable” within LLMs, stated Ann Bilyew, president of WebMD Ignite. Ads are a seemingly straightforward way to achieve that presence.

In a recent development, the problem, mentioned Bilyew, is that most of them aren’t sure how best to design the creative and messaging in a way that will let them through the “gates” of OpenAI. WebMD Ignite works directly with OpenAI, and so has more insight into the protocol and standards. “As we learn something for one health system, we’re able to apply it to all the others,” said Bilyew.

It’s too early to assert any definitive learnings, but WebMD Ignite believes that “contextual alignment will be a critical driver of performance,” Nora Simmons, VP of activation strategy, told AdExchanger.

In a recent development, chatGPT has a “relatively constrained creative format” that, for the moment, consists of an image, the brand name and a brief message, remarked Simmons, and doesn’t allow for particularly unique ad formats. As a result, she said, it’s particularly notable to ensure that the ad’s message – and then the landing page, if a user clicks on the ad – matches the intent of the user’s conversation.

It’s also crucial that the ad is “informational, not promotional,” stated Bilyew – though she acknowledged that the line between the two can be quite blurry. Generally speaking, informational ads can include specific examples of the services offered, locations and any certifications and awards they’ve received.

Healthcare marketers also aren’t immune to the challenges that all ChatGPT advertisers face: namely, knowing what sort of queries their ads appear against.

Clients can see data on views and clicks, noted Bilyew, but not on the specific content (or even types of content) that their ads appear next to. This is particularly challenging for healthcare advertisers, since ads are prohibited from appearing in any health-related conversations that are deemed sensitive or personal, making it more difficult to predict what queries they can show up against.

Determining what makes a conversation too sensitive for advertising is a subjective metric, but OpenAI told AdExchanger that even if a health condition is “strongly implied,” rather than explicitly stated, ads won’t be served during the conversation. “Someone does not need to explicitly name a diagnosis or ask for medical treatment for a conversation to fall into that sensitive category,” stated OpenAI.

For now, WebMD Ignite is optimizing its clients’ ads for informative content that doesn’t directly refer to the user’s own health conditions, such as queries like, “I’m looking to understand heart health,” said Bilyew.

WebMD Ignite also needs to have different versions of an ad for different contexts. For instance, Simmons said, a cardiology center would want to offer different messaging to someone looking to find a cardiologist versus someone asking specific questions about a particular cardiac procedure. It’s been testing roughly 100 creative variations in its early work with the cardiology division of an academic medical center, with “different messages, conversational contexts and geographic markets,” she added.

In a recent development, but one of WebMD Ignite’s greatest strengths is its willingness to admit how little is known about AI search advertising at this early stage. “We don’t know what a good budget should be in a given region,” said Bilyew, or what the delivery or inventory will look like. “We’re starting with very defined tests,” she added, and comparing the results to paid search to start assessing budget allocation on a larger scale.

Industry observers note that “Our message to clients is, ‘Look, just get in there and start learning,’” Bilyew said. “Then, as things evolve, you’ll be in a good position to evolve with it.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday.
    • Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.
    • Industry observers note that the two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Happy Thanksgiving! The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday. The Daily News Roundup will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

    Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.

    Industry observers note that the two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media. But they also can’t completely cut each other off from their respective platforms without threatening potential sales.

    In a recent development, the retail media model, which Amazon has perfected, works because it’s easy to connect ads to purchases, Shields writes. But when chatbot-based research becomes part of the customer journey, the path from ad exposure to final transaction gets much harder to trace. Just look at the IAB’s new convoluted AI attribution framework, which does what it can to try and account for the many ways AI can influence a purchase.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, Amazon realizes OpenAI is trying to steal its lunch. That’s why Amazon blocks OpenAI crawlers from accessing its retail site and prevents ChatGPT ads from linking directly to Amazon product listings.

    But not even Amazon could resist the urge to advertise on ChatGPT during the holiday shopping season, Digiday reports.

    That creates an awkward situation for Amazon, however. Its restrictions on OpenAI are also impacting how its own ad attribution works. For instance, Amazon’s ChatGPT ads direct shoppers to complete their purchase on Amazon’s site. But because they can’t click through to the product page, they have to click through to search results instead.

    And, because OpenAI can’t scrape Amazon’s site or its product pages directly, ChatGPT has to analyze info sourced from third-party deal-tracking sites to give shoppers useful advice.

    Good luck to the measurement platforms trying to make any sense of all this!

    According to recent reports, most readers may not recognize the mobile game Gossip Harbor. But its social and mobile video ads are hard to miss: horrific AI-generated scenes of marital infidelity, child neglect and animal abuse, alongside strange calls-to-action involving scenes like a mother and daughter freezing in a collapsing shelter.

    According to recent reports, the trend of AI-generated crisis ads has been covered at length, and there’s a whole economy of mobile games that redirect the resulting traffic to unrelated titles. It sounds like an implausible business model – but the numbers tell a different story.

    Sensor Tower and GameRefinery data show Gossip Harbor climbing the revenue rankings in Apple’s App Store and Google Play this year. By November, its monthly in-app revenue had topped even Candy Crush’s roughly $100 million. Mobile growth consultant Matej Lancaric has a blog post detailing the game’s revenue and marketing strategy.

    Industry observers note that aside from its ghastly creative approach, Gossip Harbor is one of the biggest games in the mobile category. What is that, you might ask? In many popular mobile merge games, players keep progressing through an ongoing story on a persistent board instead of clearing one level after another. The game is designed to go on indefinitely with regular updates.

    The ads prey on people’s anxiety to attract players, and then the games monetize the attention that follows.

    Black Friday deals just don’t hit the same way they once did – and not only because fewer people are willing to get into parking lot fistfights over them.

    It has been revealed that part of the problem, Marketing Brew argues, is that the savings are no longer relegated to a single day. Extending Black Friday into an entire month not only eases the fear of missing out, but also creates something called “promotion fatigue,” where customers are unsure about the right time to buy and may end up buying less as a result.

    According to recent reports, on top of the constant deals, customers have also become generally less trusting that they’re actually getting a bargain during the holiday season. Which makes sense because, oftentimes, they’re not.

    In a recent development, as watchdog group Groundwork Collective recently found, some retailers advertise Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals that don’t offer any significant savings. Others, meanwhile, reserve cheaper, lower-quality inventory specifically to sell during Black Friday, especially electronics.

    Recent findings suggest that so how should advertisers approach Black Friday shopping campaigns? Well, actually making the deals worthwhile would go a long way, for starters. For some companies, that might include staggering which products go on sale and when or ensuring that the prices are meaningfully low.

    Or you could just forgo the Black Friday rhetoric entirely and focus on brand-building instead, of course.

    Tidal bans AI-generated music from its platform entirely and will remove 29 million AI songs, claiming that 96% of AI tracks receive zero plays. Tidal already demonetized all AI-generated songs five months ago. [Variety].

    During an all-hands meeting discussing his comeback, returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang states the organization will hire a compliance officer “for the first time.” [post].

    Recent findings suggest that private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners has finalized its purchase of a majority stake in Puck, a digital news publisher. [The Wrap].

    Writer, podcaster and events host Alex Konrad is making his small media business work by focusing on startup founders and ventures. [Inc.].

    #171333. What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (869 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.
    • But what does performance actually mean in TV environments?
    • According to recent reports, these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in New York City on Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.

    But what does performance actually mean in TV environments? And what do media buyers need to achieve that performance?

    According to recent reports, these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in New York City on Thursday. Go Addressable is a nonprofit trade organization focused on advancing addressable TV advertising.

    Industry observers note that different advertisers typically have their own metrics for defining performance, ranging from reach and brand awareness to purchase consideration and real-life sales. But what buyers agree on is the belief that brand awareness and performance are not only connected, but causal.

    When it comes to TV and video ads, “if we don’t have scalable audiences, we can’t drive outcomes,” noted Maureen Bosetti, chief investment officer at Omnicom Media Group, speaking on a panel taking place on the Go Addressable stage.

    In other words: The entirety of the marketing funnel matters when running TV ads that aim to move money – not just lower-funnel numbers like retail sales. Hence the renewed prevalence of the term “full-funnel” in TV advertising discussions, including during this year’s upfront season.

    Industry observers note that improved measurement and transparency are at the top of buyers’ wish lists to help make TV ads work as desired. Hopefully publishers and their intermediaries will listen this time.

    When it comes to measuring video ad outcomes, the TV industry is setting itself up for disappointment because we “oversimplify” the human nature of viewers, said Jennifer Gardner, chief client solutions officer at Carat US, a subsidiary of dentsu, speaking on the same panel.

    Industry observers note that no matter how many QR codes and calls to action advertisers slap onto ad creatives, TV is still a lean-back viewing environment. At least compared with other channels and personal devices used for online shopping, such as cell phones, laptops and tablets.

    Generally speaking, TV viewers are not going to immediately pick up their phones or pause their show to run to the store when they see a commercial advertising an interesting product, Gardner noted. More often than not, viewers store that information to look into later, when they’re not in the middle of the show.

    Seeing a brand’s advertised product in the wild over time also plays a role in persuading viewers to buy something they remember seeing on TV, Gardner added. “Purchase behavior is heavily influenced by mindset,” she noted, “which is built over time.”.

    Plus, performance encompasses more than just sales. Different category verticals have their own preferred outcomes they use to gauge performance.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, fast-food and quick-service restaurants (QSR) often prioritize incremental reach as their preferred metric of performance, Bosetti remarked. For QSR brands, reach drives foot traffic, which drives business, she said, noting that QSR brands often plan media based on channels and platform most likely to reach, say, households with young children who frequent fast-food restaurants multiple times per week.

    In other words, Bosetti stated, an upper-funnel play can also be a performance-driven one.

    Despite the variances in how brands define outcomes – and how long it takes for TV to have an impact on driving those outcomes – agencies agree they need better measurement and transparency.

    Conversations pushing for better measurement and transparency have been ongoing for multiple grueling years (can confirm). Years of demands and effort toward that pursuit have led to a renewed rise in marketing mix modeling (MMM) and piecemeal upgrades in content transparency across certain publishers and their tech partners.

    Recent findings suggest that upgrades are cool. But according to agencies, they’re not enough.

    MMM is valuable, Gardner said, but it is “backward-looking” and “doesn’t tell you about changes happening in the future,” which makes it difficult for marketers to use insights from MMM before it’s too late.

    Agencies need more than just MMM to measure and optimize campaigns.

    It has been revealed that what agencies need, Bosetti stated, is standardized and “holistic” measurement that gives buyers a comprehensive view of customers and their consumption behaviors across channels, from broadcast TV and streaming to social media and online video. That comprehensive view, she said, is a core component to agencies’ ability to spot opportunities for cost-cutting and improved ad effectiveness.

    Transparency is also an crucial part of the ad measurement equation.

    In a recent development, A lot of media aims have “dead reach,” Gardner remarked, which agencies can mitigate if they have a better understanding of their target consumers. That comprehensive understanding goes beyond just audience signals and identity resolution, though, she said. According to Gardner, agencies need more detailed data from sell-side partners that capture content signals and attention data.

    Agencies want publishers to cough up more information about what viewers are actually watching and what they’re paying most attention to.

    But will they? Won’t they? Or will more debates over measurement and transparency continue to be the object of a tug-of-war game between agencies and publishers?

    Only time will tell, but don’t worry – we’re keeping close watch on this space.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led firm before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    Sources indicate that you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, launches, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    In a recent development, first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing currently works at Kit.

    According to recent reports, first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage right now routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action proposal on how we can win these creators.

    Recent findings suggest that first Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a fresh tier or add-on (nice to have).

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Recent findings suggest that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    It has been revealed that experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    In a recent development, treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    According to recent reports, wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    It has been revealed that preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Sources indicate that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance prepares through Aetna.

    According to recent reports, $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Manufacturer-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    According to recent reports, winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    Industry observers note that we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    In a recent development, we value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    • Recent findings suggest that we're looking for a Developer Relations Engineer to join our team and help more developers discover, learn, and build with Supabase.
    • It has been revealed that supabase is growing fast with 350,000+ developers, 1,000+ OSS contributors, and a thriving open source ecosystem.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Recent findings suggest that we're looking for a Developer Relations Engineer to join our team and help more developers discover, learn, and build with Supabase. You'll create high-impact content, build real-world projects, and represent Supabase across communities and events. If you're equally energized by writing code and teaching others, this is the role for you.

    It has been revealed that supabase is growing fast with 350,000+ developers, 1,000+ OSS contributors, and a thriving open source ecosystem. Our owners are builders, startup founders, weekend hackers, and engineers scaling to millions of users. DevRel is how we meet them where they are: through content, community, and code.

    In a recent development, we're building a community of communities that brings together developers from many backgrounds, including first-time open source contributors. As a DevRel Engineer, you'll be a bridge between Supabase and the broader developer ecosystem, helping people get started, go deep, and feel connected.

    Make content — Publish compelling technical content, especially video, to help developers learn Supabase swiftly.

    Build demos and tutorials — Ship real-world apps using Supabase and tools like Next.js, React, and Stripe. Write guides that others can follow and remix.

    Represent Supabase — Speak at meetups, livestream builds, and engage with the developer ecosystem. You'll be a visible and trusted voice of the platform.

    Support and grow the community — Celebrate contributors, answer questions, highlight cool projects, and bring developer feedback to the team.

    Collaborate across the company — Work with engineering, product, and growth to amplify releases, prioritize content, and reduce friction for new users.

    You've built full-stack apps and enjoy sharing your knowledge.

    You create content that makes people want to open their code editor.

    You're equally comfortable writing a video script and TypeScript.

    You're energized by community whether it's on Discord, Twitter, YouTube, or in person.

    You're self-directed, organized, and excited to contribute to open source.

    Strong engineering skills, especially with JavaScript or TypeScript, Postgres, and modern frontend frameworks (React, Svelte, Vue, etc.).

    Experience creating technical content (written or video).

    Comfortable representing a product publicly (on camera, on stage, or online).

    A growing audience on YouTube, Twitch, or Twitter.

    Prior experience in DevRel or open source.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    According to recent reports, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    It has been revealed that once a year, the entire company gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    According to recent reports, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #171305. Attorney, New Verticals at Atticus

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realworkfromanywhere ↗ Open Full Page

    Attorney, New Verticals at Atticus

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve.
    • In a recent development, so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also promptly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    In a recent development, so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

    Recent findings suggest that your job as Lead Attorney, Latest Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

    This is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the substantial picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of Upcoming Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

    On any given day, you’ll spend your time:.

    Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident.

    Sourcing and vetting local counsel in individual markets, holding a high bar for representation quality and ending relationships that fall below it.

    Working with our data and insights team to identify existing clients who may have unrecognized claims in adjacent fields of law, and setting the standard for which ancillary cases we take on.

    Building the playbook for claim types we haven't handled before, starting by screening cases yourself and eventually creating the protocol our intake specialists will run at scale.

    This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a manufacturer.

    You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

    You can empathize with anyone and promptly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

    You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You’ve built a track record as a great people manager – you know how to motivate talent and hold a high bar for output.

    You have meaningful work experience outside of serving as a lawyer, ideally at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment (e.g., a business operations team).

    We are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you're from a background that's underrepresented in tech, we'd love to meet you.

    This role offers a unique chance to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our success.

    We're a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    We anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $140,000 and $175,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    According to recent reports, this job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the company dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    • Recent findings suggest that in this role, you'll support the month-end close, perform analytics on financial results, assist with external audit and tax requests, and take on ad-hoc projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Recent findings suggest that we're looking for a detail-oriented, driven Senior Accountant to join our Accounting team at an exciting time of growth for Supabase. As we continue to scale, we're expanding the team to add experience, spread responsibilities, and strengthen the processes that keep our financials accurate and timely. This is a hands-on role with real ownership and a lot of autonomy.

    Recent findings suggest that in this role, you'll support the month-end close, perform analytics on financial results, assist with external audit and tax requests, and take on ad-hoc projects. You'll collaborate across Finance and the wider tech giant, including FP&A, People/Payroll, and Legal, and work with our external audit, tax, and technical accounting partners, while contributing to the continuous improvement of our processes and controls. This role is open to candidates based in North America.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Own key areas of the monthly, quarterly, and annual close within your assigned areas, preparing workpapers, journal entries, account reconciliations, flux analysis, and accruals in accordance with US GAAP.

    Perform detailed analytics over financial results to confirm completeness and accuracy, and investigate and communicate discrepancies promptly.

    Partner with FP&A, People/Payroll, Legal, and other teams to understand business processes, ensure proper accounting, and resolve reconciling differences.

    Support external audits and tax requests, serving as a point of contact and coordinating with external partners.

    Prepare ad-hoc analyses and support reporting requirements.

    Take initiative to recommend and implement process improvements that simplify, standardize, and streamline how we work.

    Participate in special projects, including process and system improvements.

    Handle day-to-day operational accounting activities with a high level of accuracy.

    Have 5+ years of progressive accounting experience, ideally a mix of public accounting (Big 4 preferred) and private industry.

    Have a CPA or equivalent (preferred).

    Have a strong technical accounting background and solid knowledge of US GAAP.

    Have ERP experience, and experience in tech or high-growth manufacturer accounting is a plus.

    Are willing to roll up your sleeves and dig into the details.

    Communicate clearly, both in writing and verbally, and are comfortable building relationships at all levels of the organization, including senior leadership and audit partners.

    Are self-motivated and proactive in identifying problems and proposing solutions.

    Are organized and able to manage multiple priorities and deadlines, and can switch gears rapidly in a fast-paced, high-growth environment.

    Work well both independently and collaboratively, are comfortable in async teams, and navigate ambiguity with ease.

    Are energized by improving processes.

    Recent findings suggest that we know not everyone will meet every qualification on day one. If you're excited about this role and want to grow with us, we encourage you to apply.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    In a recent development, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire company gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Sources indicate that we're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead the Pipelines team at Supabase. Supabase Pipelines is a managed change data capture product. It copies the tables you select from Supabase Postgres to other systems, then streams later changes. The product is in public alpha, with BigQuery, ClickHouse, DuckLake and Snowflake destinations.

    Pipelines uses Postgres logical replication and Supabase ETL, our open source replication engine written in Rust. The team works close to the database. That means replication slots, WAL retention, initial table syncs, and the load they place on a customer's source database. The team also builds and runs the destination connectors. Correctness, ordering and recovery matter there as much as speed.

    Recent findings suggest that the Engineering Manager is a people, delivery and technical role. We don't expect you to write production code. We do expect you to join design discussions and help set the bar for engineering quality, testing and operations.

    Build a healthy, high-trust team culture in a remote-first, globally distributed environment.

    Run 1:1s, performance management, career development, and onboarding for your direct reports.

    Surface risks, dependencies, and tradeoffs early and clearly to leadership.

    Know Postgres replication well, including logical replication, the WAL and replication slots, and how they affect a production database.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Oh yeah, GTA VI is the good stuff for streamers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that asmongold & co.
    • The long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made.
    • Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that asmongold & co. might be big mad that Grand Theft Auto VI‘s story hinges on being good to your über-hot girlfriend, but everyone else is diggin’ it.

    The long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made. It cleared $3.8 billion in sales on day one, and has the second-highest critics’ consensus rating of all time, outdone only by Nintendo‘s 1998 masterpiece The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (which just got a nice remake that released nearly in tandem with GTA VI).

    Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Twitch also saw a 33% bump in the number of channels going live: It peaked at almost ~200,000 concurrent live channels, with GTA VI making up 127,400 of them.

    YouTube Gaming, meanwhile, drew 33.2 million watch hours, and Kick generated 48.4 million.

    Now, to be clear, these are not GTA VI-specific numbers. These are across entire platforms. But it’s a good look at things holistically, because as GTA VI rose, other titles’ traffic seeped toward it.

    Sources indicate that on Twitch, GTA VI streams generated 76.81 million watch hours in the first 48 after its release. And though it didn’t include numbers, Streams Charts reports that “[h]undreds of creators also set personal audience records as fans tuned in to watch their first steps in Rockstar’s latest release.”.

    Nearly every other top title fell in watch hours, including World of Warcraft (down 31%), League of Legends (down 7%), Dota 2 (down 12%), Counter-Strike (31%), and Fortnite (39%).

    The only game that didn’t lose traction was Escape from Tarkov, which went up 11%; this is due to developer Battlestate Games holding a Twitch Drops giveaway during this timeframe, where streamers are required to broadcast Tarkov gameplay, and viewers are incentivized to tune in because they’ll get exclusive in-game items.

    The game that saw one of the biggest traffic drops was, perhaps unsurprisingly, Grand Theft Auto V, whose viewership plummeted 49%. (More on that in a minute.).

    Over on Kick, Streams Charts spotted an interesting data point: While Just Chatting streams had a 19% drop on Twitch during the first 48 hours, Kick’s Just Sleeping category jumped 176% thanks to streamers holding 24/7 GTA VI marathon streams where they left things running while they caught catnaps.

    In a recent development, things got muddy on YouTube. Streams Charts reports that many streamers went live under the GTA V category instead of GTA VI, “making it virtually impossible to separate interest in the older game from traffic driven by the new release.”.

    Streams Charts tracked YouTube watch time falls in top games like Fortnite (60%) and Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (30.4%), while Apex Legends and Free Fire rose 70% and 59%, respectively. Like with Tarkov‘s Twitch traffic, Apex and Free Fire‘s boosts were thanks to view-generating events. In Apex‘s case, it was invitational tournament FFL APEX BLOCK PARTY, and for Free Fire, it was the FFWS Global Finals 2026 competition.

    In two days, GTA VI‘s total watch hours (counted across Twitch, YouTube, Kick, and eight other platforms) beat all other game debuts’ first-week numbers.

    The closest to catching it is Valorant, which dropped in April 2020 and generated 150.48 million watch hours in its first seven days. Then there’s Elden Ring, which dropped February 2022 to 79.08M hours, and Diablo IV in June 2023 to 74.34M hours. Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk 2077, and Resident Evil Requiem are all down in the 40-60M hours range.

    Industry observers note that now, this does not mean any game will lose traffic long-term, aside from potentially GTA V. Here’s why: GTA VI is the shiny latest thing on the block. Once streamers churn through its story, most will go back to their usual niches. The ones who stick around post-campaign will be playing GTA VI Online, and those are the folks that were probably still streaming GTA V when VI came out.

    Industry observers note that GTA has one of the biggest roleplaying communities of any game, and VI provides an expansive fresh playground for folks who are into that. Everyone else will enjoy the campaign and the viewership bump it brings, then head back to Apex or WoW or League of Legends.

    • Back in March, Facebook doubled down on its efforts to woo creators from other platforms by launching Creator Fast Track—a program that pays established creators up to $3,000 a month (for a max of three months) to start posting Reels on Facebook.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Back in March, Facebook doubled down on its efforts to woo creators from other platforms by launching Creator Fast Track—a program that pays established creators up to $3,000 a month (for a max of three months) to start posting Reels on Facebook.

    Now, the Meta-owned platform is expanding that initiative to include U.S. college students with as few as 1,000 followers on Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube. Among other perks, Creator Fast Track College Edition offers eligible creators “immediate access to Facebook Content Monetization” and “increased reach on eligible reels” (per Meta).

    College students with larger followings can also access bonuses that provide “three months of guaranteed pay for sharing eligible reels.” According to Meta, “Creators with at least 20,000 followers on Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube can earn between $100-$450 per month, those with at least 100,000 followers can earn $1,000 per month, and those with more than one million followers can earn $3,000 per month.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, facebook’s creator payouts hit an all-time high last year at almost $3 billion—a 35% increase from 2024 (per Meta). Reels accounted for 60% of that total, while the rest went to Stories, photos, and text posts.

    That growing investment in creators—especially short-form video creators—is clear evidence of Facebook’s determination to compete more directly with rivals like TikTok and YouTube.

    And it’s not just targeting big-name creators, either; as Creator Fast Track’s lower entry point for college students highlights, Facebook is eager to attract young creators at the start of their careers.

    The rising importance of NIL rights and trends like #RushTok and #DormTok makes that a smart move. Since 2021, student athletes have carved out a bigger and bigger space for themselves in the creator economy, attracting the attention of major brands and platforms.

    Content creation has also become a strong Strategy B for NIL athletes who may not go pro after college. If Facebook can become a key platform for those creators while they’re still in school, it has a better shot at keeping them around after graduation—whether they go pro or pivot to full-time content creation.

    Industry News: Whatnot and Meta are taking aim at TikTok Shop’s Black Friday crown
